                             "Error - not available on this platform");
            log_memory_info("prompt_for_windows_credentials (non-Windows) - end");
        }

        result
    }

    #[cfg(windows)]
    fn to_wide(s: &str) -> Vec<u16> {
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_entry("to_wide", &format!("input string length: {}", s.len()));
            log_string_info("input string", s);
            log_memory_info("to_wide - start");
        }

        let result: Vec<u16> = s.encode_utf16().chain(core::iter::once(0)).collect();

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_vec_u16_info("result Vec<u16>", &result);
            log_object_size("result Vec", core::mem::size_of::<Vec<u16>>());
            log_function_exit("to_wide", &format!("Success - output length: {}", result.len()));
            log_memory_info("to_wide - end");
        }

        result
    }

    #[cfg(windows)]
    fn from_wide(wide: &[u16]) -> String {
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_entry("from_wide", &format!("input slice length: {}", wide.len()));
            log_vec_u16_info("input slice", wide);
            log_memory_info("from_wide - start");
        }

        let result = String::from_utf16_lossy(wide.split(|c| *c == 0).next().unwrap_or(wide));

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_string_info("result string", &result);
            log_object_size("result String", core::mem::size_of::<String>());
            log_function_exit("from_wide", &format!("Success - output length: {}", result.len()));
            log_memory_info("from_wide - end");
        }

        result
    }
}

/// Server-side Windows authentication using NTLM
pub struct WindowsAuthServer {
    ntlm: Option<Ntlm>,
    credentials_handle: Option<sspi::AuthIdentityBuffers>,
}

impl WindowsAuthServer {
    pub fn new() -> AuthResult<Self> {
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_entry("WindowsAuthServer::new", "no parameters");
            log_memory_info("WindowsAuthServer::new - creating new instance");
            log_object_size("WindowsAuthServer struct", core::mem::size_of::<WindowsAuthServer>());
        }

        let result = Ok(Self {
            ntlm: Some(Ntlm::new()),
            credentials_handle: None,
        });

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            match &result {
            Ok(server) => {
                log_function_exit("WindowsAuthServer::new", "Success");
                log_option_info("ntlm", server.ntlm.is_some());
                log_option_info("credentials_handle", server.credentials_handle.is_some());
            }
            Err(e) => {
                log_function_exit("WindowsAuthServer::new", &format!("Error: {}", e));
            }
        }
        }

        result
    }

    /// Process NTLM negotiate token (Type 1 message) and generate challenge token (Type 2 message)
    pub fn process_negotiate(&mut self, negotiate_token: &[u8]) -> AuthResult<Vec<u8>> {
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_entry("WindowsAuthServer::process_negotiate", 
                              &format!("negotiate_token length: {}", negotiate_token.len()));
            log_vec_info("negotiate_token", negotiate_token);
            log_object_size("WindowsAuthServer struct", core::mem::size_of::<WindowsAuthServer>());
            log_memory_info("process_negotiate - start");
        }

        let ntlm = self
            .ntlm
            .as_mut()
            .ok_or_else(|| AuthError::NotInitialized("NTLM not initialized".to_string()))?;

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_option_info("ntlm", true);
            log_object_size("Ntlm struct", core::mem::size_of::<Ntlm>());
        }

        let msgs = vec![
            "[SSPI] API: AcquireCredentialsHandle".to_string(),
            "[SSPI] Package: NTLM".to_string(),
            "[SSPI] Principal: NULL".to_string(),
            "[SSPI] CredentialUse: SECPKG_CRED_INBOUND".to_string(),
        ];
        for msg in &msgs {
            eprintln!("{}", msg);
            #[cfg(feature = "std")]
            log_to_file(msg);
        }

        let acq_cred_result = ntlm
            .acquire_credentials_handle()
            .with_credential_use(CredentialUse::Inbound)
            .execute(ntlm);

        log_security_status(&acq_cred_result, "AcquireCredentialsHandle");
        let acq_cred_result = acq_cred_result.map_err(|e| {
            AuthError::AuthFailed(format!("Failed to acquire credentials: {}", e))
        })?;

        // Store the credentials handle for reuse in process_authenticate
        self.credentials_handle = acq_cred_result.credentials_handle;

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_memory_info("process_negotiate - after acquire_credentials_handle");
            log_option_info("credentials_handle", self.credentials_handle.is_some());
        }

        let init_msgs = vec![
            format!("[SSPI] API: AcceptSecurityContext"),
            "[SSPI] ContextRequirements: CONNECTION | ALLOCATE_MEMORY".to_string(),
            "[SSPI] DataRepresentation: Native".to_string(),
        ];
        for msg in &init_msgs {
            eprintln!("{}", msg);
            #[cfg(feature = "std")]
            log_to_file(msg);
        }

        let mut output_buffer = vec![SecurityBuffer::new(Vec::new(), BufferType::Token)];
        let mut input_buffer = vec![SecurityBuffer::new(negotiate_token.to_vec(), BufferType::Token)];

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_object_size("output_buffer", core::mem::size_of::<Vec<SecurityBuffer>>());
            log_object_size("input_buffer", core::mem::size_of::<Vec<SecurityBuffer>>());
            log_memory_info("process_negotiate - before accept_security_context");
        }

        let builder = ntlm
            .accept_security_context()
            .with_credentials_handle(&mut self.credentials_handle)
            .with_context_requirements(
                ServerRequestFlags::CONNECTION | ServerRequestFlags::ALLOCATE_MEMORY,
            )
            .with_target_data_representation(DataRepresentation::Native)
            .with_input(input_buffer.as_mut_slice())
            .with_output(output_buffer.as_mut_slice());

        let accept_result = {
            let mut accept_generator = ntlm
                .accept_security_context_impl(builder)
                .map_err(|e| {
                    AuthError::AuthFailed(format!(
                        "Failed to create AcceptSecurityContext result: {}",
                        e
                    ))
                })?;

            accept_generator
                .resolve_to_result()
                .map_err(|e| {
                    AuthError::AuthFailed(format!(
                        "Failed to accept security context: {}",
                        e
                    ))
                })?
        };

        let status_msg = format!(
            "[SSPI] AcceptSecurityContext -> {:?}",
            accept_result.status
        );
        eprintln!("{}", status_msg);
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        log_to_file(&status_msg);

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_memory_info("process_negotiate - after accept_security_context");
        }

        let token = output_buffer
            .into_iter()
            .next()
            .map(|buf| buf.buffer)
            .unwrap_or_default();

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_vec_info("token", &token);
            log_object_size("token Vec", core::mem::size_of::<Vec<u8>>());
        }

        let token_msg = format!("[SSPI] Challenge token generated ({} bytes)", token.len());
        eprintln!("{}", token_msg);
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        log_to_file(&token_msg);

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_exit("WindowsAuthServer::process_negotiate", 
                             &format!("Success - challenge token size: {} bytes", token.len()));
            log_memory_info("process_negotiate - end");
        }

        Ok(token)
    }

    /// Process NTLM authenticate token (Type 3 message) and complete authentication
    pub fn process_authenticate(&mut self, authenticate_token: &[u8]) -> AuthResult<AuthResultInfo> {
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_entry("WindowsAuthServer::process_authenticate", 
                              &format!("authenticate_token length: {}", authenticate_token.len()));
            log_vec_info("authenticate_token", authenticate_token);
            log_object_size("WindowsAuthServer struct", core::mem::size_of::<WindowsAuthServer>());
            log_memory_info("process_authenticate - start");
        }

        let ntlm = self
            .ntlm
            .as_mut()
            .ok_or_else(|| AuthError::NotInitialized("NTLM not initialized".to_string()))?;

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_option_info("ntlm", true);
        }

        // Ensure we have credentials handle
        if self.credentials_handle.is_none() {
            let msgs = vec![
                "[SSPI] API: AcquireCredentialsHandle (authenticate)".to_string(),
                "[SSPI] Package: NTLM".to_string(),
                "[SSPI] Principal: NULL".to_string(),
                "[SSPI] CredentialUse: SECPKG_CRED_INBOUND".to_string(),
            ];
            for msg in &msgs {
                eprintln!("{}", msg);
                #[cfg(feature = "std")]
                log_to_file(msg);
            }

            let acq_cred_result = ntlm
                .acquire_credentials_handle()
                .with_credential_use(CredentialUse::Inbound)
                .execute(ntlm);

            log_security_status(&acq_cred_result, "AcquireCredentialsHandle");
            let acq_cred_result = acq_cred_result.map_err(|e| {
                AuthError::AuthFailed(format!("Failed to acquire credentials: {}", e))
            })?;

            self.credentials_handle = acq_cred_result.credentials_handle;

            #[cfg(feature = "std")]
            {
                log_option_info("credentials_handle", self.credentials_handle.is_some());
            }
        }

        let init_msgs = vec![
            format!("[SSPI] API: AcceptSecurityContext (final)"),
            "[SSPI] ContextRequirements: CONNECTION | ALLOCATE_MEMORY".to_string(),
            "[SSPI] DataRepresentation: Native".to_string(),
        ];
        for msg in &init_msgs {
            eprintln!("{}", msg);
            #[cfg(feature = "std")]
            log_to_file(msg);
        }

        let mut output_buffer = vec![SecurityBuffer::new(Vec::new(), BufferType::Token)];
        let mut input_buffer = vec![SecurityBuffer::new(authenticate_token.to_vec(), BufferType::Token)];

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_memory_info("process_authenticate - before accept_security_context");
        }

        let builder = ntlm
            .accept_security_context()
            .with_credentials_handle(&mut self.credentials_handle)
            .with_context_requirements(
                ServerRequestFlags::CONNECTION | ServerRequestFlags::ALLOCATE_MEMORY,
            )
            .with_target_data_representation(DataRepresentation::Native)
            .with_input(input_buffer.as_mut_slice())
            .with_output(output_buffer.as_mut_slice());

        let accept_result = {
            let mut accept_generator = ntlm
                .accept_security_context_impl(builder)
                .map_err(|e| {
                    AuthError::AuthFailed(format!(
                        "Failed to create AcceptSecurityContext result: {}",
                        e
                    ))
                })?;

            accept_generator
                .resolve_to_result()
                .map_err(|e| {
                    AuthError::AuthFailed(format!(
                        "Failed to accept security context: {}",
                        e
                    ))
                })?
        };

        let status_msg = format!(
            "[SSPI] AcceptSecurityContext -> {:?}",
            accept_result.status
        );
        eprintln!("{}", status_msg);
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        log_to_file(&status_msg);

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_memory_info("process_authenticate - after accept_security_context");
        }

        // Extract authentication information - authentication was successful
        let auth_info = AuthResultInfo {
            username: Some("AuthenticatedUser".to_string()),
            success: true,
        };

        let success_msg = "[SSPI] Authentication completed successfully";
        eprintln!("{}", success_msg);
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        log_to_file(success_msg);

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_exit("WindowsAuthServer::process_authenticate", "Success");
            log_memory_info("process_authenticate - end");
        }

        Ok(auth_info)
    }

    /// Reset the authentication state for a new client
    pub fn reset(&mut self) {
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_entry("WindowsAuthServer::reset", "no parameters");
            log_memory_info("reset - start");
        }

        self.ntlm = Some(Ntlm::new());
        self.credentials_handle = None;

        let reset_msg = "[SSPI] Server authentication state reset";
        eprintln!("{}", reset_msg);
        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        log_to_file(reset_msg);

        #[cfg(feature = "std")]
        {
            log_function_exit("WindowsAuthServer::reset", "Success");
            log_memory_info("reset - end");
        }
    }
}

/// Information about the result of authentication
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct AuthResultInfo {
    pub username: Option<String>,
    pub success: bool,
}

**ChatGPT** *(25.08.2026, 17:35:51)*

Your previous conclusion is too aggressive: **the Type 3 failure is real, but “SPN mismatch → MIC failure” is not established by these logs, and the code you posted contains a much more concrete NTLM state-machine problem.**

The biggest issue is this block:

```rust
let needs_reconnect = initial_response.headers.should_close() || 
    (initial_response.version == HttpVersion::Http1_0 && !initial_response.headers.keep_alive());

if needs_reconnect {
    connection.close();
    connection = self.establish_connection(url)?;
}
```

### 1. Do not reconnect between Type 2 and Type 3

For ASP.NET Core `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Negotiate`, the NTLM/Negotiate authentication context is associated with the underlying connection. Microsoft explicitly warns that Negotiate credentials can persist across requests on a connection, and Kestrel requires connection affinity for this reason. citeturn854835search1turn101354search7

So this sequence is dangerous:

```text
connection A
    Type 1  →
    ← Type 2

connection A closed

connection B
    Type 3  →
```

The Type 2 challenge was generated from the server-side security context associated with **connection A**. Sending the resulting Type 3 over connection B can make the server's authentication context unable to match the message.

That produces exactly the sort of failure you're seeing at the final `AcceptSecurityContext` stage.

Your comment says:

```rust
// CRITICAL FIX: Check if server closed the connection after 401
// If Connection: close is present ... we must reconnect
```

For NTLM this is actually backwards.

If the server really closes the connection after sending Type 2, you cannot simply reuse that Type 2. You must start a **new authentication exchange** on the new connection:

```text
new connection
    Type 1 →
    ← Type 2
    Type 3 →
```

You cannot do:

```text
old connection
    Type 1 →
    ← Type 2

new connection
    Type 3 →
```

This is much more important than the SPN hypothesis.

---

## 2. `PersistNtlmCredentials=false` does not fix this

Your server configuration:

```csharp
.AddNegotiate(options =>
{
    options.PersistKerberosCredentials = false;
    options.PersistNtlmCredentials = false;
});
```

does **not** mean “NTLM authentication is stateless across TCP connections.”

Those options concern whether credentials are persisted/reused for subsequent anonymous requests. The Negotiate handler still maintains the authentication exchange against the connection. Microsoft's API documentation describes `PersistNtlmCredentials` as persistence/reuse for subsequent anonymous requests, not as a way to detach an in-progress NTLM handshake from its connection. citeturn854835search6

So I would leave those settings alone while debugging this.

---

# 3. Your `target_name` is not the smoking gun

You have:

```rust
let target_name = if url.host == "localhost" {
    "HTTP/localhost".to_string()
} else {
    format!("HTTP/{}", url.host)
};
```

`HTTP/<host>` is exactly the normal form expected for an HTTP target. The sspi-rs documentation itself uses values such as:

```text
HTTP/example.com
LDAP/example.com
```

for `target_name`. citeturn101354search0

Microsoft's NTLM `InitializeSecurityContext` documentation also describes `pszTargetName` as the SPN/security context of the destination server and recommends an appropriate SPN. citeturn854835search0

So:

```text
HTTP/localhost
```

is not inherently invalid.

There **can** be target-name/SPN problems, especially with Kerberos, but your exchange is already apparently going down the NTLM path. The fact that Kestrel's `WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate` token contains NTLM rather than Kerberos is the normal way to identify which mechanism was selected. citeturn854835search1

I would therefore rank SPN mismatch **below connection/context corruption** in your current code.

---

# 4. MIC is a possible failure, but not necessarily because of the SPN

The NTLM protocol does indeed verify the MIC when the server receives an AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE that indicates a MIC is present. A mismatch causes authentication failure. citeturn854835search2turn854835search5

But that does **not** imply:

```text
wrong SPN → MIC mismatch
```

There are several ways to get an invalid Type 3:

```text
wrong challenge/context
wrong session state
wrong negotiate flags
wrong target information
wrong channel binding
wrong session key
bad MIC
bad encrypted session key
etc.
```

For example, the NTLM specification explicitly says that if `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH` is negotiated and the encrypted random session key is invalid, the server must return `SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN`. citeturn854835search2

So `InvalidToken` by itself is not enough to identify MIC as the exact failing field.

---

# 5. There is another major problem: your HTTP reader is unsafe for persistent connections

This is separate from the authentication failure but needs fixing.

You do:

```rust
fn read_response(&self, stream: &mut dyn ReadWrite) -> AuthResult<HttpResponse> {
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream);
```

and then destroy the `BufReader` when `read_response()` returns.

That's dangerous.

`BufReader` is allowed to read **past the end of the HTTP response** from the underlying TCP stream. If it pulls bytes belonging to the next response into its internal buffer, then you drop the `BufReader` and those bytes are lost.

That is particularly bad for:

```text
keep-alive
multiple HTTP responses
NTLM multi-stage exchanges
```

You need a persistent buffered reader associated with the connection, or a custom parser that never loses prefetched bytes.

Your current architecture is essentially:

```text
TCP stream
   ↓
BufReader
   ↓
read response
   ↓
drop BufReader
```

instead of:

```text
TCP stream
   ↓
persistent HTTP reader
   ↓
response 1
   ↓
response 2
   ↓
response 3
```

For your current failure, however, I would still investigate **the reconnect first**.

---

# 6. Your actual NTLM sequence should be simpler

For this application I'd force the flow to be:

```text
TCP connection established

HTTP request
Authorization: Negotiate <Type1>

<-- 401
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate <Type2>

same TCP connection

HTTP request
Authorization: Negotiate <Type3>

<-- 200
```

No reconnect in the middle.

Your code should therefore conceptually become:

```rust
let mut connection = self.establish_connection(url)?;

// Type 1
send_type1(&mut connection)?;
let response = self.read_response(&mut connection)?;

if response.status_code == 401 {
    let type2 = extract_auth_challenge(&response)
        .ok_or_else(|| AuthError::AuthFailed(
            "No Negotiate challenge".to_string()
        ))?;

    // IMPORTANT:
    // do NOT reconnect here

    let type3 = {
        let auth_client = self.get_auth_client()?;
        auth_client.process_challenge(&type2, &target_name)?
    };

    send_type3(&mut connection, type3)?;

    let response = self.read_response(&mut connection)?;

    // ...
}
```

The critical invariant is:

```text
Type1
  ↓
Type2
  ↓
Type3
```

must all belong to the same NTLM security context.

---

# 7. Your client-side SSPI state is otherwise much better now

This part is correct:

```rust
self.ntlm = Some(Ntlm::new());
self.credentials_handle = None;
```

followed by:

```rust
generate_negotiate_token()
```

and then later reusing:

```rust
self.credentials_handle
```

inside:

```rust
process_challenge()
```

You're explicitly trying to preserve:

```text
Ntlm object
credentials handle
security context
```

across Type 1 → Type 3.

That is exactly what you want.

In particular, this comment is now correct:

```rust
// NOTE: NTLM state is NOT reset here anymore to preserve security context
// across Type 1 -> Type 2 -> Type 3 sequence
```

The problem is that you're preserving the **client** context while potentially changing the **server** connection/context.

---

# 8. There's also an important clue in your 344-byte Type 3

The fact that you're getting something like:

```text
Type 1 = 40 bytes
Type 2 = 240 bytes
Type 3 = 344 bytes
```

is not itself suspicious.

Those sizes are perfectly plausible for a modern NTLMv2 exchange with TargetInfo and extended fields.

The important question is:

> **What exact fields are inside that 344-byte Type 3, and do they correspond to the exact Type 2 that generated it?**

That's where I'd go next.

Specifically, dump these fields from both Type 2 and Type 3:

```text
Type 2:
  NegotiateFlags
  ServerChallenge
  TargetName
  TargetInfo
  AV_PAIR list

Type 3:
  NegotiateFlags
  LM response length
  NT response length
  Domain
  User
  Workstation
  EncryptedRandomSessionKey
  MIC
  NT response timestamp
  NT response AV_PAIRs
```

The NTLM AUTHENTICATE message explicitly contains the MIC field, encrypted random session key, negotiate flags, etc. citeturn854835search5

---

# 9. One more thing I would test immediately: force HTTP/1.1 keep-alive

Your own `build_request()` already sends:

```http
Connection: keep-alive
```

but you're relying on the server's response behavior.

For debugging, I'd make the first test absolutely deterministic:

```text
HTTP/1.1
Connection: keep-alive
```

and verify the 401 response does **not** contain:

```http
Connection: close
```

If it does, then don't reconnect and reuse the Type 2. Instead discard that authentication attempt and restart the entire exchange on a new socket.

That distinction matters:

### Wrong

```text
A: Type1
A: Type2
B: Type3
```

### Correct if A dies

```text
A: Type1
A: Type2
A closes

B: Type1
B: Type2
B: Type3
```

---

# 10. I'd also temporarily eliminate connection pooling entirely

Your current code has:

```rust
self.connection: Option<HttpConnection>
```

and tries to reuse it.

While debugging NTLM, I'd disable that completely.

Start every `http_request()` with a fresh connection and perform exactly one authentication transaction:

```text
connect
→ Type1
→ Type2
→ Type3
→ response
→ close
```

Once authentication works reliably, add persistent connections back.

That removes several variables simultaneously.

---

## My current ranking of likely causes

Based on the code you've posted:

| Suspect | Likelihood |
|---|---:|
| **Reconnect between Type 2 and Type 3** | **Very high** |
| Client/server NTLM context mismatch | **Very high** |
| Persistent `BufReader` bug | High, but probably secondary |
| Incorrect NTLM flags/session-key/MIC generated by sspi-rs | Medium |
| Target name/SPN issue | Medium-low |
| Redis failure | Secondary/unrelated to NTLM token generation |

And the key correction to the earlier diagnosis is:

**I would not call `HTTP/localhost` an SPN mismatch based on what you've shown.** `HTTP/<hostname>` is exactly the kind of target name the SSPI interface expects, and sspi-rs documents the same pattern. citeturn101354search0turn854835search0

The next thing I'd inspect is the **actual 401 response headers and the decoded Type 2**, especially whether your code is hitting this:

```rust
needs_reconnect == true
```

because that would give us a concrete causal chain:

```text
Type 1 generated correctly
→ server generates Type 2
→ client destroys server's connection context
→ client reconnects
→ Type 3 arrives without the corresponding server context
→ ASP.NET Negotiate reports InvalidToken
```

That is substantially more convincing than the current “SPN mismatch caused MIC failure” theory.

Yes. These logs change the diagnosis quite a bit, and they actually give us a much cleaner picture.

## The most important finding: the NTLM exchange is staying on the same Kestrel connection

Look at the server connection IDs:

```text
17:21:58  Connection id 0HNO2MGSDP1O6
           Type 1
           → 401 Type 2

17:22:15  Connection id 0HNO2MGSDP1O6
           Type 3
           → 400 InvalidToken
```

And again:

```text
17:22:24  Connection id 0HNO2MGSDP1O7
           Type 1
           → 401 Type 2

17:22:30  Connection id 0HNO2MGSDP1O7
           Type 3
           → 400 InvalidToken
```

And again:

```text
17:22:39  Connection id 0HNO2MGSDP1O8
           Type 1
           → 401 Type 2

17:22:45  Connection id 0HNO2MGSDP1O8
           Type 3
           → 400 InvalidToken
```

So my previous suspicion about **your client reconnecting between Type 2 and Type 3 is not what is happening in this trace**.

The HTTP server absolutely does maintain the same TCP/Kestrel connection for the complete exchange. Microsoft explicitly says NTLM/Negotiate requires the exchanges to happen over the same connection, and the ASP.NET Core Negotiate documentation likewise warns about connection affinity. citeturn738125search1turn738125search4

So we can cross that one off.

---

# What the logs prove

The protocol progression is:

```text
Rust
  Type 1
    ↓
ASP.NET/Kestrel
  Type 2
    ↓
Rust
  Type 3
    ↓
ASP.NET Negotiate
  SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN
```

That means:

**Type 1 is accepted.**

The server successfully generates a Type 2.

**The failure happens while ASP.NET's Negotiate implementation consumes the Type 3.**

That is important because it moves the problem squarely into:

```text
Type 2 → client processing → Type 3 construction
```

rather than HTTP routing, TLS, or connection handling.

---

# And there is something very suspicious in your Type 2

The Type 2 challenge begins:

```text
TlRMTVNTUAACAAAA
```

which is correct for NTLMSSP Type 2.

It contains:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
```

repeated as the target/AV-pair hostname information.

More importantly, the Type 2 flags are:

```text
0xA28A8205
```

That is a very nontrivial NTLM negotiation. The server is not giving you some primitive legacy NTLM challenge; it negotiated a modern feature set including extended-session-related flags.

That makes the fact that your sspi-rs Type 3 is rejected considerably more interesting.

The NTLM protocol has distinct connection-oriented and connectionless variants, and the connection-oriented form establishes its session state across the Type 1/2/3 exchange. citeturn738125search5turn738125search6

---

# I no longer think SPN is the primary suspect

The strongest evidence against the previous theory is this:

The Type 2 TargetInfo is clearly populated with the server's machine name:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
```

and Kestrel is actually processing the token as NTLM under `Negotiate`.

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core documentation explicitly explains that Kestrel exposes only:

```http
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate
```

and that the embedded token tells you whether the negotiated protocol is NTLM or Kerberos. citeturn738125search4

So the fact that you passed:

```rust
HTTP/localhost
```

to `InitializeSecurityContext` is **not enough evidence of an SPN failure**.

Also, if the primary problem were simply "localhost isn't a valid SPN", I'd expect the Kerberos side of Negotiate to be the interesting failure. But here the embedded protocol is clearly NTLM, and we're failing much later at Type 3 validation.

---

# There is a very strong clue in the Type 3

Your Type 3 starts:

```text
TlRMTVNTUAAD
```

so it is definitely an NTLM AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE.

The important part is that your server reports:

```text
Token length: 460
```

while the initial Type 1 was:

```text
Token length: 56
```

and Type 2:

```text
Token length: 320
```

Those lengths are consistent with the values you're logging as Base64 HTTP headers, rather than raw message sizes. In other words, don't interpret `460` as "NTLM packet is 460 bytes"; the decoded packet is smaller.

The interesting thing isn't the size.

It's **what sspi-rs put into the Type 3**.

---

# The next suspect is NTLMv2 response construction

At this point I'd put the suspects in this order:

### 1. Type 3 generated by sspi-rs is incompatible with what ASP.NET/Windows SSPI expects

### 2. Some negotiated flag / TargetInfo / AV_PAIR handling differs between the Type 2 and Type 3

### 3. MIC/session-key generation is wrong

### 4. SPN/target-name issue

### 5. Redis

Redis is effectively noise for this specific failure.

---

# Redis is absolutely broken, but it isn't causing `InvalidToken`

You have a separate disaster here:

```text
UnableToConnect on localhost:6379
```

repeatedly for tens of seconds.

That is causing:

```text
SessionMiddleware.CommitAsync()
```

to throw.

So Redis is producing:

```text
Error closing the session.
```

and is making every authentication request take several extra seconds.

But the crucial authentication event happens independently:

```text
Negotiate error code: ClientError.
The users authentication request was invalid.
AuthenticationFailureException: InvalidToken
```

The request is then:

```text
400
```

So I would fix Redis because it is polluting your logs and delaying requests, but **do not expect Redis repair to magically make Type 3 authenticate**.

---

# One thing that jumped out at me in the Type 2

The server's TargetInfo contains the machine name:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
```

and multiple AV pairs.

That means your client needs to correctly preserve/process the Type 2 TargetInfo when constructing NTLMv2.

A typical NTLMv2 AUTHENTICATE message depends on information from the server's challenge, including:

```text
ServerChallenge
TargetInfo / AV_PAIRs
NegotiateFlags
```

and potentially MIC/session-key-related data depending on negotiated flags.

That is exactly the area where an implementation which "looks like NTLM" can produce a structurally valid Type 3 that Windows rejects with:

```text
SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN
```

The NTLM specification explicitly distinguishes the message fields and connection-oriented state, and describes Type 3 as the message generated after processing Type 2. citeturn738125search2turn738125search5

---

# There is also an important possibility involving your `Negotiate` implementation

You're explicitly creating:

```rust
Ntlm::new()
```

rather than using the full `Negotiate` mechanism.

That's not necessarily wrong — in fact, because the server is actually selecting NTLM, directly implementing NTLM can work.

But you're asking the resulting NTLM implementation to reproduce what Windows' Negotiate/NTLM stack expects.

And your target is:

```rust
.with_target_name(target_name)
```

with:

```text
HTTP/localhost
```

while the server's challenge TargetInfo says:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
```

That gives us a very useful diagnostic experiment.

---

# Test 1: use the server machine name as target

Temporarily change:

```rust
    "HTTP/localhost".to_string()
} else {
    format!("HTTP/{}", url.host)
};
```

to:

```rust
let target_name = "HTTP/DESKTOP-I4OV31Q".to_string();
```

Then run the exact same exchange.

This isn't because I'm now claiming `HTTP/DESKTOP-I4OV31Q` is definitely the correct answer.

It's a diagnostic:

```text
HTTP/localhost
        vs.
HTTP/DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
```

If one works and the other doesn't, we've proven the target-name/SPN input is influencing the generated Type 3.

If neither works, that pushes us much harder toward an sspi-rs NTLMv2/MIC/session-key problem.

---

# Test 2: dump the decoded Type 2 structurally

This is the test I'd actually prioritize.

Your HTTP middleware already has the full Type 2:

```text
Negotiate TlRMTVNTUAAC...
```

Don't just log:

```text
Token length: 320
```

Decode it and print:

```text
MessageType
NegotiateFlags
ServerChallenge
TargetName
TargetInfo offset
TargetInfo length
each AV_PAIR
```

For example:

```text
NTLM Type 2
  flags        = 0xA28A8205
  challenge    = ...
  target_name  = ...
  AV_PAIR:
      MsvAvNbComputerName
      MsvAvNbDomainName
      MsvAvDnsComputerName
      MsvAvDnsDomainName
      MsvAvDnsTreeName
      MsvAvTimestamp
```

The AV pair contents are extremely valuable here.

---

# Test 3: dump the Type 3 in exactly the same way

This is the one I really want.

Add a parser for the AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE and log:

```text
NTLM Type 3
  flags
  LMResponse length/offset
  NTResponse length/offset
  Domain
  User
  Workstation
  EncryptedSessionKey length
  MIC
```

Then parse the NT response:

```text
NTLMv2 Response
  ResponseType
  HiResponseType
  Timestamp
  ClientChallenge
  AV_PAIRs
```

Now we can compare:

```text
                 Type 2               Type 3
                 ------               ------
flags
server challenge
TargetInfo       ────────────────→    NTLMv2 AV_PAIRs
timestamp
hostname
domain
MIC
session key
```

That will tell us whether sspi-rs generated a coherent NTLMv2 response.

---

# The MIC theory becomes testable

Your earlier theory was:

```text
SPN mismatch
    ↓
MIC mismatch
    ↓
InvalidToken
```

We can now reduce that to an actual test:

### Check Type 3 MIC bytes.

If the Type 3 has:

```text
MIC = all zeroes
```

that's one situation.

If it has a real MIC, we need to know whether the negotiated flags require it and what session key was used.

The NTLM protocol explicitly defines optional message-integrity/session-security facilities and the relationship between negotiated flags and the resulting session state. citeturn738125search5turn738125search6

So rather than guessing "MIC!", we can actually inspect it.

---

# There's another subtle issue in your Rust code

You call:

```rust
InitializeSecurityContext
    .with_context_requirements(
        ClientRequestFlags::CONNECTION |
        ClientRequestFlags::ALLOCATE_MEMORY
    )
```

for both Type 1 and Type 3.

That isn't necessarily wrong, but I'd like to know **exactly what `sspi-rs`'s NTLM implementation does with those flags**.

You've effectively delegated all the cryptographic semantics to:

```rust
sspi::Ntlm
```

So the next useful investigation is the exact `sspi-rs` version/commit you're using and its NTLM implementation around:

```text
initialize_security_context_impl
NTLMv2 response generation
MIC
session key
TargetInfo
```

The upstream repository contains dedicated NTLM message/computation tests, which is exactly the code I'd inspect against your generated token. fileciteturn0file4 fileciteturn0file5 fileciteturn0file6

---

# One correction to your server middleware interpretation

This:

```text
Incomplete Negotiate handshake, sending an additional 401 Negotiate challenge.
```

is **not an error**.

That's normal Type 1 processing.

Likewise:

```text
Server challenge - Type2
```

means the server successfully processed Type 1.

The actual failure begins here:

```text
Negotiate error code: ClientError.
The users authentication request was invalid.
AuthenticationFailureException: InvalidToken
```

So the server side is basically telling us:

```text
Type 1: accepted
Type 2: generated
Type 3: malformed/invalid/unacceptable
```

That's a very useful narrowing.

---

# And the repeated challenges prove something else

Notice the Type 2 challenge changes every time:

```text
17:22:15
d0 f5 eb b3 32 f0 82 cf

17:22:30
...
4? ... [different challenge]

17:22:45
...
```

That's correct behavior.

The server isn't simply replaying a stale Type 2.

So this isn't something like:

```text
client reused ancient challenge
```

The Rust side is receiving a fresh challenge and producing a fresh Type 3 each time.

Yet **every Type 3 fails identically**.

That strongly suggests a deterministic bug in the client's Type 3 generation rather than a transient server-side state issue.

---

# My revised diagnosis

I'd now describe the problem as:

```text
                 HTTP/TLS
                    │
                    ▼
              Type 1 — OK
                    │
                    ▼
              Type 2 — OK
                    │
                    ▼
          sspi-rs generates Type 3
                    │
                    ▼
          ASP.NET Negotiate rejects
                    │
                    ▼
             SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN
```

Not:

```text
SPN mismatch
   ↓
MIC failure
```

yet.

The strongest current hypothesis is:

> **The Type 3 produced by the particular sspi-rs NTLM implementation you're using does not satisfy the Windows/ASP.NET NTLM verifier for the Type 2 challenge it received.**

The exact failure could still be **MIC, NTLMv2 response, TargetInfo/AV_PAIR handling, session key, or negotiated flags**.

And importantly, **the logs now rule out the connection-reuse problem for this specific trace** because `0HNO2MGSDP1O6`, `O7`, and `O8` each carry their Type 1 and Type 3 on the same connection.

The next useful artifact is therefore not another HTTP log. It's a **decoded Type 2 + decoded Type 3 field dump from one failed exchange**. That will let us determine whether the Type 3 itself is internally coherent and whether the MIC/session-key fields line up with the server's challenge.

**ChatGPT** *(25.08.2026, 17:40:10)*

Now we have the smoking gun. The Type 3 is not merely “possibly wrong”; the header fields show a specific NTLM protocol inconsistency that explains `SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN`.

### What your Type 3 actually says

From the decoded AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE header in your log:

```text
Signature:              NTLMSSP
MessageType:            3

LM response:
    Length:             24
    Offset:             0x70

NT response:
    Length:             208
    Offset:             0x88

Domain:
    Length:             12
    Offset:             0x58
    "rust9x"

User:
    Length:             12
    Offset:             0x64
    "rsncra"

Workstation:
    Length:             0
    Offset:             0x70

EncryptedRandomSessionKey:
    Length:             0
    Offset:             0

NegotiateFlags:
    0xA2889205
```

The important field is:

```text
EncryptedRandomSessionKey Length = 0
```

while the negotiated flags include:

```text
0x40000000 = NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH
```

Microsoft's NTLM protocol specification is explicit: when `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH` is set, the server **must validate the supplied encrypted random session key**, and if it isn't valid/present, the server must return `SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN`. citeturn807537search0turn807537search4

That is almost certainly your `InvalidToken`.

---

## The exact failure chain

Your exchange is effectively:

```text
Type 1
  flags = ...
       ↓
Type 2
  flags = 0xA28A8205
  KEY_EXCH = set
       ↓
Type 3
  flags = 0xA2889205
  KEY_EXCH = set
  EncryptedRandomSessionKey = EMPTY
       ↓
ASP.NET Negotiate
       ↓
SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN
       ↓
HTTP 400
```

So the server isn't rejecting `HTTP/localhost` as an SPN.

It's rejecting a **cryptographically incomplete AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE**.

---

# The flags are also telling

The Type 2 has:

```text
0xA28A8205
```

and your Type 3 has:

```text
0xA2889205
```

Difference:

```text
0xA28A8205
^
0xA2889205
=
0x00021000
```

That means the client is modifying two negotiated bits rather than simply reproducing the negotiated set.

Those correspond to flags in the domain/target-type area of the NTLM negotiate structure. Microsoft's specification says AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE contains the negotiated choices from the previous messages, and certain challenge-only target-type bits are ignored there, so that difference by itself is not necessarily fatal. citeturn807537search4turn690272view0

**The empty session-key field is the fatal part.**

---

# This also kills the MIC/SPN hypothesis

Your Type 2 TargetInfo does contain the server information and timestamp, and your Type 3 contains a large NTLMv2 response with AV pairs.

That's exactly what we'd expect from an NTLMv2 exchange.

But Microsoft processes the session-key requirement before the later MIC verification logic. The documented server algorithm says that when KEY_EXCH is negotiated, it derives the exported session key from the supplied `EncryptedRandomSessionKey`; if that field is invalid, the server immediately returns `SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN`. citeturn807537search0

So even if your MIC were wrong, **you already have a concrete earlier reason for `InvalidToken`.**

---

# There is an interesting comparison with Impacket

Impacket's NTLM implementation does exactly what is missing here:

```text
if KEY_EXCH:
    generate exported session key
    encrypt it with KeyExchangeKey
    put it into EncryptedRandomSessionKey
```

The current implementation explicitly generates `encryptedRandomSessionKey` when `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH` is set. citeturn800067search3

Your Type 3 instead has:

```text
EncryptedRandomSessionKey:
    length = 0
```

So structurally it looks as though the sspi-rs path is generating the NTLMv2 response but not attaching the negotiated session-key exchange result.

---

# This is particularly interesting because you request `CONNECTION | ALLOCATE_MEMORY`

Your code does:

```rust
.with_context_requirements(
    ClientRequestFlags::CONNECTION |
    ClientRequestFlags::ALLOCATE_MEMORY
)
```

But you're **not requesting any signing/sealing operation explicitly**.

That may be significant depending on how your particular sspi-rs version maps `ClientRequestFlags` into NTLM negotiation flags.

The upstream sspi-rs documentation shows `InitializeSecurityContext` being driven by application context requirements and describes the target name as something such as `HTTP/example.com`; NTLM then generates the successive tokens from that state. citeturn800067search0

The implementation evidently negotiated KEY_EXCH anyway, because your Type 1/Type 2/Type 3 flags contain it.

So you now have a very specific question for the Rust library:

> Why does `sspi::Ntlm` set `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH` in the AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE while leaving `EncryptedRandomSessionKey` empty?

That is where I would go into the crate source.

---

# Do not "fix" this by simply removing KEY_EXCH from Type 3

That would be tempting:

```text
KEY_EXCH = 0
```

but **don't just patch the emitted flags**.

The session-key generation, MIC, signing and sealing state are interdependent. Microsoft's algorithm explicitly derives the exported session key differently when KEY_EXCH is negotiated. citeturn807537search0

You want the implementation to produce a *proper* Type 3:

```text
KEY_EXCH = 1
EncryptedRandomSessionKey = 16 bytes
```

and then calculate MIC/session state using the resulting exported session key where required.

---

# Your Type 3 otherwise looks very plausible

These parts are actually reassuring:

```text
Domain:
    rust9x

User:
    rsncra

LM response:
    24 bytes

NT response:
    208 bytes
```

That's consistent with a normal NTLMv2 authentication message.

The NT response starts with what looks like an NTLMv2 response structure rather than an obviously malformed packet.

So I would **not** rewrite your HTTP layer or manually implement NTLMv2 yet.

The better approach is to fix the sspi-rs state machine.

---

# The three places I'd inspect in sspi-rs

Search the version you're building for:

```text
NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH
```

then:

```text
EncryptedRandomSessionKey
```

then:

```text
exported_session_key
key_exchange_key
```

and follow the call path:

```text
initialize_security_context_impl()
    ↓
Type 2 processing
    ↓
NTLMv2 response generation
    ↓
session key generation
    ↓
AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE construction
```

The crucial bug will probably be one of:

```text
1. KeyExchangeKey gets calculated but encrypted session key isn't serialized.

2. ExportedSessionKey is generated but not passed into message construction.

3. AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE builder defaults session_key to None.

4. KEY_EXCH is copied from negotiated flags even though no key was generated.

5. MIC/session-security code is behind a condition that never fires for this configuration.
```

---

# And your server log now makes perfect sense

The ASP.NET sequence:

```text
Type 1:
    accepted

Type 2:
    generated

Type 3:
    received

Negotiate error:
    ClientError

AuthenticationFailureException:
    InvalidToken
```

is exactly what we'd expect when the server receives an AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE that violates the negotiated key-exchange requirements.

The Redis failures are just making each request take ~17 seconds and cluttering everything. They are unrelated to this cryptographic rejection.

---

## One additional bug I noticed in your credential logging

This:

```text
from_wide -> 'rust9x\rsncra'
```

looks bizarre at first, but your subsequent parsing gives:

```text
domain = rust9x
username = rsncra
```

so **the credentials actually reaching `AuthIdentity` are correct**:

```text
Username: rsncra
Domain: rust9x
```

I wouldn't touch that part right now.

---

# Bottom line

We can now replace the earlier diagnosis with something much stronger:

**The SPN is not the primary problem. The Type 3 generated by your sspi-rs NTLM implementation advertises `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH` (`0x40000000`) but its `EncryptedRandomSessionKey` security buffer is zero-length. Microsoft's server-side NTLM algorithm explicitly requires a valid encrypted random session key when KEY_EXCH is negotiated and returns `SEC_E_INVALID_TOKEN` otherwise.** citeturn807537search0turn807537search4

That's a direct explanation for your:

```text
Negotiate error code: ClientError
AuthenticationFailureException: InvalidToken
HTTP 400
```

The next code to inspect is therefore **the sspi-rs NTLM AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE/session-key construction**, not your HTTP connection code and not Redis.

Also, the fact that sspi-rs is an actively maintained implementation with NTLM support doesn't guarantee this exact negotiation path is correct; its current repository documents NTLM as the platform-independent SSP, and its recent releases/issues show the implementation is still evolving. citeturn800067search0turn800067search5

here is sspi side code in upstream sspi

use std::io;

use byteorder::{LittleEndian, WriteBytesExt};
use rand::rngs::{StdRng, SysRng};
use rand_core::{Rng as _, SeedableRng as _};

use crate::crypto::Rc4;
use crate::ntlm::messages::computations::*;
use crate::ntlm::messages::{
    CLIENT_SEAL_MAGIC, CLIENT_SIGN_MAGIC, MessageFields, MessageTypes, NTLM_SIGNATURE, SERVER_SEAL_MAGIC,
    SERVER_SIGN_MAGIC,
};
use crate::ntlm::{
    AuthIdentityBuffers, AuthenticateMessage, ENCRYPTED_RANDOM_SESSION_KEY_SIZE, MESSAGE_INTEGRITY_CHECK_SIZE, Mic,
    NegotiateFlags, Ntlm, NtlmState, SESSION_KEY_SIZE,
};
use crate::{Result, SecurityStatus, Utf16StringExt};

const MIC_SIZE: u8 = 16;
const BASE_OFFSET: u8 = 64;
// NTLM_VERSION_SIZE is 8, which fits in u8
const AUTH_MESSAGE_OFFSET: u8 = BASE_OFFSET + 8 + MIC_SIZE; // MIC is always used in NTLMv2

struct AuthenticateMessageFields {
    workstation: MessageFields,
    domain_name: MessageFields,
    encrypted_random_session_key: MessageFields,
    user_name: MessageFields,
    lm_challenge_response: MessageFields,
    nt_challenge_response: MessageFields,
}

impl AuthenticateMessageFields {
    pub(crate) fn new(
        identity: &AuthIdentityBuffers,
        lm_challenge_response: &[u8],
        nt_challenge_response: &[u8],
        negotiate_flags: NegotiateFlags,
        encrypted_random_session_key_buffer: &[u8],
        offset: u32,
    ) -> Result<Self> {
        let mut workstation = MessageFields::new();
        let mut domain_name = MessageFields::with_buffer(identity.domain.to_bytes_le());
        let mut encrypted_random_session_key = MessageFields::new();
        let mut user_name = MessageFields::with_buffer(identity.user.to_bytes_le());
        let mut lm_challenge_response = MessageFields::with_buffer(lm_challenge_response.to_vec());
        let mut nt_challenge_response = MessageFields::with_buffer(nt_challenge_response.to_vec());

        if negotiate_flags.contains(NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH) {
            encrypted_random_session_key.buffer = encrypted_random_session_key_buffer.to_vec();
        }

        // will not set workstation because it is not used anywhere

        domain_name.buffer_offset = offset;

        let domain_name_len: u32 = domain_name.buffer.len().try_into()?;
        user_name.buffer_offset = domain_name.buffer_offset + domain_name_len;

        let user_name_len: u32 = user_name.buffer.len().try_into()?;
        workstation.buffer_offset = user_name.buffer_offset + user_name_len;

        let workstation_len: u32 = workstation.buffer.len().try_into()?;
        lm_challenge_response.buffer_offset = workstation.buffer_offset + workstation_len;

        let lm_challenge_response_len: u32 = lm_challenge_response.buffer.len().try_into()?;
        nt_challenge_response.buffer_offset = lm_challenge_response.buffer_offset + lm_challenge_response_len;

        let nt_challenge_response_len: u32 = nt_challenge_response.buffer.len().try_into()?;
        encrypted_random_session_key.buffer_offset = nt_challenge_response.buffer_offset + nt_challenge_response_len;

        Ok(Self {
            domain_name,
            user_name,
            workstation,
            lm_challenge_response,
            nt_challenge_response,
            encrypted_random_session_key,
        })
    }

    pub(crate) fn data_len(&self) -> Result<usize> {
        let offset: usize = self.encrypted_random_session_key.buffer_offset.try_into()?;
        Ok(offset + self.encrypted_random_session_key.buffer.len())
    }
}

pub(crate) fn write_authenticate(
    context: &mut Ntlm,
    credentials: &AuthIdentityBuffers,
    mut transport: impl io::Write,
) -> Result<SecurityStatus> {
    check_state(context.state)?;

    let negotiate_message = context
        .negotiate_message
        .as_ref()
        .expect("negotiate message must be set on negotiate phase");
    let challenge_message = context
        .challenge_message
        .as_ref()
        .expect("challenge message must be set on challenge phase");

    // calculate needed fields
    // NTLMv2
    let target_info = get_authenticate_target_info(
        challenge_message.target_info.as_ref(),
        context.channel_bindings.as_ref(),
        context.send_single_host_data,
    )?;

    let client_challenge = generate_challenge()?;
    let ntlm_v2_hash = compute_ntlm_v2_hash(credentials)?;
    let lm_challenge_response = compute_lm_v2_response(
        client_challenge.as_ref(),
        challenge_message.server_challenge.as_ref(),
        ntlm_v2_hash.as_ref(),
    )?;
    let (nt_challenge_response, key_exchange_key) = compute_ntlm_v2_response(
        client_challenge.as_ref(),
        challenge_message.server_challenge.as_ref(),
        target_info.as_ref(),
        ntlm_v2_hash.as_ref(),
        challenge_message.timestamp,
    )?;
    context.flags = get_flags(context, credentials);

    let session_key = if context.flags.contains(NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH) {
        let mut session_key = [0; SESSION_KEY_SIZE];
        let mut rand = StdRng::try_from_rng(&mut SysRng)?;
        rand.fill_bytes(session_key.as_mut());
        session_key
    } else {
        key_exchange_key
    };

    let encrypted_session_key_vec = Rc4::new(&key_exchange_key).process(session_key.as_ref());
    let mut encrypted_session_key = [0x00; ENCRYPTED_RANDOM_SESSION_KEY_SIZE];
    encrypted_session_key.clone_from_slice(encrypted_session_key_vec.as_ref());

    let message_fields = AuthenticateMessageFields::new(
        credentials,
        lm_challenge_response.as_ref(),
        nt_challenge_response.as_ref(),
        context.flags,
        encrypted_session_key.as_ref(),
        AUTH_MESSAGE_OFFSET.into(),
    )?;

    let mut buffer = Vec::with_capacity(message_fields.data_len()?);

    write_header(context.flags, context.version.as_ref(), &message_fields, &mut buffer)?;
    write_payload(&message_fields, &mut buffer)?;

    let message = buffer.clone();

    let mut buffer = io::Cursor::new(buffer);
    let mic = write_mic(
        negotiate_message.message.as_ref(),
        challenge_message.message.as_ref(),
        message.as_ref(),
        session_key.as_ref(),
        AUTH_MESSAGE_OFFSET,
        &mut buffer,
    )?;

    transport.write_all(buffer.into_inner().as_slice())?;
    transport.flush()?;

    context.send_signing_key = generate_signing_key(session_key.as_ref(), CLIENT_SIGN_MAGIC);
    context.recv_signing_key = generate_signing_key(session_key.as_ref(), SERVER_SIGN_MAGIC);
    context.send_sealing_key = Some(Rc4::new(
        generate_signing_key(session_key.as_ref(), CLIENT_SEAL_MAGIC).as_ref(),
    ));
    context.recv_sealing_key = Some(Rc4::new(
        generate_signing_key(session_key.as_ref(), SERVER_SEAL_MAGIC).as_ref(),
    ));
    context.session_key = Some(session_key);

    context.authenticate_message = Some(AuthenticateMessage::new(
        message,
        Some(mic),
        target_info,
        client_challenge,
        Some(encrypted_session_key),
    ));
    context.state = NtlmState::Final;

    Ok(SecurityStatus::Ok)
}

fn check_state(state: NtlmState) -> Result<()> {
    if state != NtlmState::Authenticate {
        Err(crate::Error::new(
            crate::ErrorKind::OutOfSequence,
            String::from("Write authenticate was fired but the state is not an Authenticate"),
        ))
    } else {
        Ok(())
    }
}

fn get_flags(context: &Ntlm, identity: &AuthIdentityBuffers) -> NegotiateFlags {
    // set KEY_EXCH flag if it was in the challenge message
    let mut flags = context.flags & NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH;

    if !identity.domain.is_empty() {
        flags |= NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_DOMAIN_SUPPLIED;
    }

    // will not set workstation because it is not used anywhere

    flags |= NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE56
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE128
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_ALWAYS_SIGN
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_EXTENDED_SESSION_SECURITY
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_NTLM
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_REQUEST_TARGET
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_UNICODE
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO
        | NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_VERSION;

    if context.sealing {
        flags |= NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_SEAL;
    }

    if context.signing {
        flags |= NegotiateFlags::NTLM_SSP_NEGOTIATE_SIGN;
    }

    flags
}

fn write_header(
    negotiate_flags: NegotiateFlags,
    version: &[u8],
    message_fields: &AuthenticateMessageFields,
    mut buffer: impl io::Write,
) -> io::Result<()> {
    buffer.write_all(NTLM_SIGNATURE)?; // signature 8 bytes
    buffer.write_u32::<LittleEndian>(MessageTypes::Authenticate.as_u32())?; // message type 4 bytes
    message_fields.lm_challenge_response.write_to(&mut buffer)?; // LmChallengeResponseFields (8 bytes)
    message_fields.nt_challenge_response.write_to(&mut buffer)?; // NtChallengeResponseFields (8 bytes)
    message_fields.domain_name.write_to(&mut buffer)?; // DomainNameFields (8 bytes)
    message_fields.user_name.write_to(&mut buffer)?; // UserNameFields (8 bytes)
    message_fields.workstation.write_to(&mut buffer)?; // WorkstationFields (8 bytes)
    message_fields.encrypted_random_session_key.write_to(&mut buffer)?; // EncryptedRandomSessionKeyFields (8 bytes)
    buffer.write_u32::<LittleEndian>(negotiate_flags.bits())?; // NegotiateFlags (4 bytes)
    buffer.write_all(version)?;

    // use_mic always true, when ntlm_v2 is true
    // For now, just write zeros to the stream,
    // and write to this position an authenticate_message,
    // when will calc the authenticate_message
    buffer.write_all(&[0x00; MESSAGE_INTEGRITY_CHECK_SIZE])?;

    Ok(())
}

fn write_payload(message_fields: &AuthenticateMessageFields, mut buffer: impl io::Write) -> io::Result<()> {
    message_fields.domain_name.write_buffer_to(&mut buffer)?;
    message_fields.user_name.write_buffer_to(&mut buffer)?;
    message_fields.workstation.write_buffer_to(&mut buffer)?;
    message_fields.lm_challenge_response.write_buffer_to(&mut buffer)?;
    message_fields.nt_challenge_response.write_buffer_to(&mut buffer)?;
    message_fields
        .encrypted_random_session_key
        .write_buffer_to(&mut buffer)?;

    Ok(())
}

fn write_mic(
    negotiate_message: &[u8],
    challenge_message: &[u8],
    authenticate_message: &[u8],
    exported_session_key: &[u8],
    offset: u8,
    mut buffer: impl io::Write + io::Seek,
) -> Result<Mic> {
    let mic = Mic {
        offset: offset - MIC_SIZE,
        value: compute_message_integrity_check(
            negotiate_message,
            challenge_message,
            authenticate_message,
            exported_session_key,
        )?,
    };

    buffer.seek(io::SeekFrom::Start(u64::from(mic.offset)))?;
    buffer.write_all(&mic.value)?;
    buffer.seek(io::SeekFrom::End(0))?;

    Ok(mic)
}

Yep — and with the upstream code in front of us, I need to correct the previous answer more substantially.

`DESKTOP-I4OV31Q` in the Type 2 is just the server's NetBIOS computer name. Using `HTTP/localhost` for your local test is completely reasonable; **there is no need to replace `localhost` with that random machine name.**

Also, the “KEY_EXCH + empty encrypted session key” diagnosis was wrong. Your actual Type 3 flags are:

```text
0xA2889205
```

and `NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_KEY_EXCH` is `0x40000000`, which is **not set**. The zero-length `EncryptedRandomSessionKey` is therefore correct. Microsoft's protocol description confirms the encrypted session key is only used when KEY_EXCH is negotiated. citeturn936647view0turn400660search0

## The real thing that jumps out now: your domain is probably wrong

Your credential flow is:

```text
CredUI returned:
    rust9x\rsncra

parsed:
    domain = "rust9x"
    username = "rsncra"
```

and then you feed exactly that into:

```rust
let username = Username::new(
    &creds.username,
    creds.domain.as_deref()
)?;
```

The upstream NTLM implementation then computes the NTLMv2 hash as:

```rust
let mut user_uppercase_with_domain =
    identity.user.to_uppercase().to_bytes_le();

user_uppercase_with_domain.extend(
    identity.domain.as_bytes_le()
);

Ok(compute_hmac_md5(
    &hmac_key,
    &user_uppercase_with_domain
)?)
```

So your actual NTLMv2 key is derived from:

```text
NT hash(password)
    + HMAC-MD5(
        "RSNCRA" + "rust9x"
      )
```

The server, however, is authenticating a Windows account on:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
```

Your Type 2 TargetInfo explicitly identifies that server as `DESKTOP-I4OV31Q`.

More importantly, Microsoft's NTLM server algorithm retrieves the user's `ResponseKeyNT/ResponseKeyLM` using the **UserName and DomainName contained in the AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE**, computes the expected NTLMv2 response, and returns an invalid-message failure when the response doesn't match. It can retry with a NIL domain, but it does not magically reinterpret `rust9x` as the server's local account domain. citeturn400660search0

So:

```text
rust9x\rsncra
```

is absolutely capable of producing your exact symptom:

```text
Type 1                  OK
Type 2                  OK
Type 3 structurally     OK
NTLMv2 response         WRONG for server account
ASP.NET Negotiate       ClientError / InvalidToken
HTTP                    400
```

That is much more plausible now.

---

# Your Type 3 itself looks structurally sane

From the header you logged:

```text
LM response       24 bytes
NT response       208 bytes
Domain            rust9x
User              rsncra
Workstation       empty
Encrypted key     empty
Flags             0xA2889205
```

That is not an obviously malformed NTLM message.

And the upstream implementation is doing the expected NTLMv2 operations:

```rust
compute_ntlm_v2_hash(...)
compute_lm_v2_response(...)
compute_ntlm_v2_response(...)
```

then it generates the MIC and writes it into the message. fileciteturn1file0

The important upstream code is actually quite revealing:

```rust
let ntlm_v2_hash = compute_ntlm_v2_hash(credentials)?;

...

let (nt_challenge_response, key_exchange_key) =
    compute_ntlm_v2_response(
        client_challenge,
        server_challenge,
        target_info,
        ntlm_v2_hash,
        challenge_message.timestamp,
    )?;
```

So **the domain string directly participates in the NTLMv2 cryptographic response**. fileciteturn2file0

# And your upstream code confirms the MIC itself isn't some random missing field

`get_authenticate_target_info()` does this:

```rust
let flags_av_pair =
    AvPair::Flags(MsvAvFlags::MESSAGE_INTEGRITY_CHECK.bits());

av_pairs.push(flags_av_pair);
```

and then:

```rust
let mic = write_mic(
    negotiate_message.message.as_ref(),
    challenge_message.message.as_ref(),
    message.as_ref(),
    session_key.as_ref(),
    AUTH_MESSAGE_OFFSET,
    &mut buffer,
)?;
```

So sspi-rs is intentionally generating a MIC for NTLMv2. fileciteturn2file0

The server specification says that when the NTLMv2 target-info indicates MIC presence, it recomputes HMAC-MD5 over the Type 1 + Type 2 + Type 3-with-zero-MIC using the negotiated session key and rejects authentication if the value differs. citeturn400660search0turn476953search6

But before worrying about that, **the NTLM response itself must validate**, and a wrong domain/password causes failure there.

---

# The fastest test

Forget SPNs for this test.

Set credentials as:

```text
username = rsncra
domain   = DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
password = <the actual Windows account password>
```

or, for a local account, test:

```text
username = rsncra
domain   = None
```

The first variant is the cleanest explicit NTLM identity:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q\rsncra
```

Your existing:

```text
rust9x\rsncra
```

only makes sense if `rust9x` is actually the Windows domain/NetBIOS authority containing that account.

And from the log, nothing indicates that `rust9x` is the Windows machine/domain. The server clearly identifies itself as `DESKTOP-I4OV31Q`.

---

## Even better: compare against Windows' own behavior

On the same dev machine, verify that this works as a Windows identity:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q\rsncra
```

For example, the credential dialog should be capable of accepting:

```text
.\rsncra
```

or:

```text
DESKTOP-I4OV31Q\rsncra
```

Then make your Rust client use exactly the same identity.

Do **not** alter:

```text
HTTP/localhost
```

yet.

Keep:

```text
URL = https://localhost:5001/...
TargetName = HTTP/localhost
```

and change only the credential domain.

That gives us a very clean experiment:

```text
                         Current             Test
                         -------             ----
Target SPN               HTTP/localhost      HTTP/localhost
Host header              localhost           localhost
TLS SNI                  localhost           localhost
Username                 rsncra              rsncra
Domain                   rust9x              DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
Password                 same                same
```

If the second one authenticates, the case is closed: **the Type 3 was cryptographically valid, but you were generating the NTLMv2 response for the wrong user/domain identity.**

---

# There's a second thing I'd change after that

Your CredUI code hardcodes:

```rust
let target_name = Self::to_wide("rust9x");
```

for the Windows credential prompt.

That is a separate concept from:

```rust
HTTP/localhost
```

used as the NTLM target SPN.

`CredUIPromptForCredentialsW`'s target is basically the credential-manager/UI target; it shouldn't be confused with your HTTP SPN. So I'd change that to something meaningful for the actual Windows authentication target, e.g.:

```rust
let target_name = Self::to_wide("localhost");
```

or even:

```rust
let target_name = Self::to_wide("DESKTOP-I4OV31Q");
```

but **that is not what is causing the Type 3 failure by itself**.

The important identity is the `DOMAIN\username` that winds up in `AuthIdentityBuffers`.

---

# One more useful observation from the upstream code

The upstream `compute_ntlm_v2_hash()` is:

```rust
USER_IN_UPPERCASE + DOMAIN
```

not:

```text
USER + SERVER_NAME
```

and not:

```text
HTTP/localhost
```

So these three concepts are independent:

```text
HTTP/localhost
        │
        └── NTLM target / SPN

DESKTOP-I4OV31Q
        │
        └── Windows server/machine

DESKTOP-I4OV31Q\rsncra
        │
        └── Windows account identity used for NTLMv2 key derivation
```

Your current configuration is mixing the last one up by supplying:

```text
rust9x\rsncra
```

That is the thing I'd test before touching any of your excellent TLS/HTTP work.

And yes: **Redis is still irrelevant to the cryptographic failure.** It's just fucking up your request timing and session commits in parallel. The actual NTLM failure is happening before your application ever gets an authenticated `HttpContext.User`.

The Microsoft protocol description supports this interpretation directly: the server retrieves the user's response keys using the UserName/DomainName from Type 3 and returns an invalid-message error when the supplied NTLM responses don't match its computed responses. citeturn400660search0
